title: The lord and the servant (ch. 51)
hook: a servant falls into a ditch rushing to serve, and the lord looks on him with love
tomorrow: if prayer doesn't get you what you asked for, what's it for?

segments.voice: A week of two short classics. Lawrence: no fuss, and a little lifting. Julian: sixteen showings, love was his meaning, mother Jesus. And yesterday's promise, said three times over: all manner of thing shall be well.
screen: `NO FUSS · A LITTLE LIFTING.` → `SIXTEEN SHOWINGS · LOVE WAS HIS MEANING.` → `MOTHER JESUS · ALL MANNER OF THING.`

segments.voice: You sprint to catch a door for someone with full arms, and you trip on the curb. Now you're the one on the ground, and the person you meant to help is staring down at you. Julian of Norwich was shown a story much like that: a servant who runs to do his lord's will, and falls into a ditch on the way.
screen: `SPRINTING TO HOLD THE DOOR.` → `DOWN ON THE CURB.` → `A SERVANT IN A DITCH.`

segments.voice: In chapter fifty-one, a lord sits in rest and peace, and a servant stands ready. The lord sends him, and the servant doesn't walk. He runs, in haste, for love, to do his lord's will. And he falls into a slade, a hollow in the ground, and is badly hurt. Julian notices the worst of it. He groans, and he can't turn his face to see his lord, who is right there. He feels alone. And the lord? He looks on the servant with pity and love, not blame, because the fall came from his good will. Julian says she took years to understand what she'd been shown. In the servant she came to see Adam, which means all of us, and also Christ, who comes down into our ditch. Look how the week gathers here: a fall met without fuss, love as the meaning, a mother who holds, and all shall be well, in one picture.
screen: `HE RUNS, FOR LOVE.` · `INTO THE DITCH.` · `HE CAN'T SEE HIS LORD'S FACE.` · `THE LORD LOOKS WITH LOVE.` · then, large: `HE FELL RUSHING TO SERVE.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers three falls from this past month, small ones. For each, name what you were rushing toward when you fell: helping, finishing, pleasing someone. Then rest, and let the lord's look in Julian's story, the one with no blame in it, rest on all three.
The lord and the servant. Julian's story of a servant hurt while rushing to serve, and a lord who looks on him with love.
screen: `THE LORD AND THE SERVANT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Pocket this one: he fell rushing to serve, and the look he got had no blame in it. That's the week.

howItsDone: Catholics reading Julian often linger on this chapter as a picture of how God sees human failure; it is read alongside the Church's teaching on the Fall and on Christ's coming.

notes: Chapter 51 paraphrased: the lord sits solemnly in rest and peace; the servant stands ready; sent, he goes not only but suddenly starts and runs in great haste, for love, to do his lord's will; he falls into a slade and takes full great hurt; he groans and moans, and his greatest hurt is that he cannot turn his face to look on his loving lord, who is full near; he is alone; the lord beholds him with pity and ruth, without blame, because only his good will and great desire caused the fall. Julian's later understanding: in the servant she sees Adam (all humankind) and the Son, Christ; and her note that the teaching came some twenty years after the showing, here given only as 'years later'. Confirm wording.
